extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of physics and philosophy of science (readers of a conceptual textbook on mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual/textbook treatment of the Newtonian laws of motion and their domain, expressing how to construct mechanical models (corpuscles, ether, fields, frames) and the limitations of those assumptions. Focuses on what assumptions to make about interactions, inertia, frames, and the role of velocity as past history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain of applicability of laws of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Question how far laws that describe the relative motion of two particles should be conceived as holding for two molecules, two chemical atoms, two prime-atoms, and ultimately for two ether-elements; whether laws for gross 'matter' result from how particles are built up from smaller constituents or whether they hold down to the ether-element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always state explicitly to which ideal corpuscles (particle, molecule, atom, prime-atom, ether-element) your laws are supposed to apply; do not uncritically extend kinetic/special laws (gravitation, magnetisation, electrification, heat/light emission/absorption) beyond the structural domain from which they plausibly flow. Consider whether mechanism is an emergent property of ascending complexity or a general property extending to the ether.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Law of Motion (universal mutual influence with distance-dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every corpuscle in the conceptual model of the universe must be conceived as moving with due regard to the presence of every other corpuscle, although for very distant corpuscles the regard paid is extremely small compared with that paid to immediate neighbours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modelling, assume mutual influence among corpuscles but quantify or treat distant influences as negligible when appropriate. Provide alternative formulations (direct action at a distance vs. mediation via adjacent ether-elements) and be explicit which is being used in the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field isolation and neglect of negligible influences
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing conceptual models we isolate a particular group of corpuscles (the 'field') and neglect at once influences which even in the aggregate are beyond our powers of measurement; we exclude slight measurable variations due to more distant groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the field size and justify omissions of distant influences by measurement limits. Use this criterion to simplify models: isolate systems only after verifying the aggregate influence omitted is below perceptual/instrumental significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of inertia (Second Law conceptual statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more completely we separate one corpuscle from the influence of other corpuscles, the more nearly does its motion relative to a suitable frame cease to vary: the corpuscle either remains at rest relative to this frame or continues to move with the same speed in the same direction (uniform motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In models, attribute inertia to corpuscles as the rule that uniform motion is unaltered except in presence of other corpuscles. Be careful to state the limiting assumptions (negligible external influences, choice of frame) under which inertia is asserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame of reference selection and its practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'frame' is fixed by corpuscles at such a distance that their influence is insensible; for practical purposes a frame determined by the stars or the solar system is used, but these frames are approximations and have theoretical/practical objections (stars not truly fixed, uncertain distances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state what frame is used for relative motion (stars, solar system, ether) and acknowledge limitations/approximations. For refined astronomical work, account for slight variations; for ordinary problems the 'fixed' star/solar frame is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of inertia to ether-elements vs gross matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of inertia probably applies from the prime-atom to the particle, but may not apply (or has different meaning) for ether-elements: if prime-atoms depend on ether-elements the isolated-corpuscle thought-experiment becomes absurd and inertia for gross matter may flow from its internal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking inertia, state whether it is assumed as a structural property of gross matter or as a property deduced from interactions with an ether; avoid transferring the same inertia assumption uncritically to conceptual ether-elements without defining the ether model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual accelerations determined by relative position (Third Law conceptualization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual accelerations of corpuscles have the same direction but opposite senses, and (usually assumed) this direction is that of the line joining the corpuscles: knowledge of relative position determines accelerations (rates of change of relative position), not velocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt that mutual accelerations are equal and opposite; for many particle models take acceleration along the line joining them. But clearly state when this 'central' assumption is made and justify it by the scale and type of particles being modelled (non-adjacent particles, point approximations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations for extended bodies and groups (when line-joining assumption fails)
rubrics_metrics.description: For prime-atoms, molecules, or groups where point approximation is invalid, the line joining two corpuscles is meaningless and one must deal with relative motion of groups of elements; similarly adjacent ether-elements challenge the central-line picture if the ether is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For systems where physical dimensions are comparable to separation, replace point-particle central-force assumptions by models of interacting groups or continua (surface motions, extended-element interactions). Explicitly check the validity of point approximations before applying central-force reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible dependence of mutual acceleration on relative velocities (ether/fluid mediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual accelerations may depend not only on relative position but also on relative velocities (as when bodies move in a fluid); conservation of energy proofs often assume accelerations depend only on position, but apparent velocity-dependence can be reconciled by including the mediating medium's energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to include velocity-dependent interaction terms (e.g., hydrodynamic/ether-mediated forces). If velocity dependence is observed or suspected, model the mediating medium as part of the system so conservation laws hold for the combined system; do not claim violation of conservation without accounting for unmodelled medium energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: General statement on acceleration dependence (practical rule for gross matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general the acceleration of a point-symbolising element will depend on its position relative to other elements (and possibly on velocities); for particles of gross 'matter' it is generally (if not invariably) sufficient to assert dependence solely on relative position and conceive accelerations as taking place in the line joining two particles in opposite senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use position-only dependence as a working rule for modelling gross matter unless there is specific evidence necessitating velocity-dependent terms (electromagnetic, aerodynamic, or medium-coupled phenomena). Explicitly note this assumption in derivations and predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity as epitome of past history and determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Given actual velocities of all corpuscles and how accelerations depend on relative position (and possibly velocity), one can in theory reconstruct past histories and future evolution of the system; velocity summarises past changes of motion and encodes antecedent causes in the conceptual model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat initial velocities as compact encodings of past interactions and as necessary initial data for deterministic prediction. Acknowledge practical limitations (measurement limits, computational intractability) when asserting theoretical determinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism as conceptual description, not metaphysical materialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical models are conceptual descriptions of the changes we perceive, not explanations proving materialism; mechanical descriptions, however successful, should not be conflated with metaphysical claims that laws are 'inherent in things themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanism pragmatically as an instrument for prediction and description; avoid overinterpreting model success as philosophical proof of materialism. State clearly when using models as heuristic tools versus making ontological claims.
